summary: Documents security concerns with IP tunnels and proposes strategies for mitigating them, to raise awareness among administrators and protocol developers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Tunnels let traffic travel hidden inside other traffic, which can bypass safety checks. This lists the dangers and how to reduce them.

subtitle: Security threats and mitigations for IP traffic tunneled over UDP or TCP.

tldr.problem: IP tunnels encapsulate packets inside UDP or TCP to traverse NATs and firewalls, but this creates security gaps: tunneled traffic bypasses network security controls, contents are hard to inspect, NAT openings increase attack surface, and tunnel addresses reveal information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6169 identifies specific threats: network-based controls cannot see inner IP headers, ingress/egress filtering is bypassed, NAT mappings become stable open holes, and guessable tunnel addresses enable profiling. The RFC proposes operational and protocol-design mitigations for each.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators and protocol developers gain awareness of tunnel security implications. Operators can disable tunnels, enforce host-based firewalls, or require authentication. Protocol designers can randomize addresses and ports, disable tunneling in restricted networks, or support better tunnel endpoint authentication.

today: RFC 6169 is an informational guidance document that remains highly relevant. Tunnel-based circumvention and IPv6 transition mechanisms continue to be deployed. Network administrators and security teams reference this RFC when evaluating tunnel policies and configuring controls.

sections.title: Why Tunnels Are Risky
sections.content:
IP tunneling encapsulates IP packets inside another IP packet (or UDP/TCP) to traverse network boundaries like NATs, firewalls, or security appliances. Protocols like Teredo, L2TPv2/L2TPv3, and SSL VPNs tunnel IP over UDP or TCP to reach the Internet from behind restrictive networks. This creates unintended security consequences.

The primary concern is that tunneled traffic bypasses network-based security controls. A firewall or intrusion detection system (IDS) inspecting outer headers sees only UDP/TCP traffic; it does not recognize that an inner IP packet is embedded. Unless the security device specifically understands the tunnel protocol, the embedded packets escape inspection and policy application.

Network defense relies on defense in depth: multiple layers of security. When tunnels bypass network-layer controls, the depth is reduced. Even if host-based firewalls exist, security administrators may not have configured them with full parity to network policies, leaving security gaps.

This is particularly concerning because many network administrators may not even realize their hosts are globally reachable through tunnels. A host behind a stateful firewall that lacks tunnel awareness becomes unexpectedly exposed to Internet attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunnels hide packets inside UDP or TCP so they get through firewalls. But if the firewall does not understand the tunnel, it cannot check what is really being sent. It is like hiding a letter inside a package: the mail room checks packages, but nobody opens them to see the letter.

sections.title: How Tunnels Bypass Security
sections.content:
Network security bypass: Tunneled IP traffic does not receive the intended level of inspection by network-based security devices unless they are tunnel-aware. Security developers face a lag between recognizing a new tunnel protocol and implementing support, testing it, releasing an update, and having customers deploy it. During this lag, tunnels are undefended.

IP ingress and egress filtering bypass: Ingress filtering prevents packets with internal source addresses from entering from outside; egress filtering prevents internal packets from leaving with spoofed external addresses. These are network-level controls applied at domain boundaries. Tunneled IP addresses are not subject to this filtering because they are encapsulated inside the outer packet. Only the tunnel endpoints can filter the inner addresses.

Source routing after tunnel client: If an encapsulated IP packet contains source routing directives (specifying the next hop), the tunnel client host may forward it to that hop, potentially unexpected to the administrator and contrary to network-level source-routing controls. The RFC recommends tunnel clients discard source-routed packets by default.

The cumulative effect is that a host globally reachable through a tunnel presents a larger attack surface. The processing chain before the inner IP is reached includes link-layer, outer IP, UDP/TCP, and tunnel processing. Vulnerabilities in any of these could be exploited; a worm needing only one UDP packet and a remote code vulnerability could spread across tunneled hosts without native IP exposure.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewalls check outer envelopes but tunnels hide real packages inside. IP filters do not understand the inside address is wrong. Malicious routing instructions in the hidden packet could make the host forward it somewhere unexpected.

sections.title: Inspecting and Filtering Tunneled Traffic
sections.content:
Difficulty identifying all tunneled packets: Some tunnel protocols (like 6to4) use a well-known IP protocol number and are easy to identify. Others use dynamic UDP/TCP ports or share ports with non-tunneled traffic. Network devices cannot efficiently and immediately filter all tunneled packets. Blocking a single well-known port (e.g., 3544 for Teredo) prevents new tunnels but not existing ones using different ports. Filtering tunnel server IP addresses works if servers are stable but is impractical for consumer services.

Deep packet inspection overhead: To inspect all tunneled traffic, network devices must examine all TCP/UDP packets and attempt to parse each as a potential tunnel. Using heuristics (e.g., check if the packet contains a valid inner IP header and has matching source/destination), devices can identify tunnels but at high computational cost. This may require taking packets off the fast path, reducing throughput.

Practical limitations: The RFC observes that inspecting tunneled traffic is highly complex and often impractical. Administrators unable to disable tunnels on hosts cannot rely on efficient network-level filtering. The recommendation is to avoid tunneling across security boundaries (e.g., do not tunnel through a perimeter firewall). Instead, tunneling should be contained within networks or use tunnel solutions that terminate inside the network, not at global Internet servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tunnels use obvious ports, but others hide. Checking every packet to see if it is a tunnel is slow and unreliable. Better to not allow tunnels across your firewall in the first place, or to use tunnels that end inside your network.

sections.title: Increased Attack Surface from NAT Holes
sections.content:
NAT hole increase: When a tunnel is active, a mapped port is maintained on the NAT device. Remote hosts can send packets through this hole. The tunnel client receives these packets and processes them through multiple layers: link-layer, outer IP firewall, outer IP stack, UDP/TCP stack, tunnel processing, inner IP firewall, and inner IP stack. Vulnerabilities in any layer before the inner firewall could be exploited. Even if the inner firewall blocks the packet, the processing cost and attack surface are larger than native IP.

Stable, discoverable holes: Unlike typical NAT mappings that come and go, tunnel mappings are held open for extended periods. This increases discovery probability. In some protocols like Teredo, the external IP address and port are embedded in the tunnel address itself, making them discoverable through address analysis or DNS. Attackers see more packet exchanges with tunnels than native IP, offering more visibility into ports and addresses.

Public Internet tunnels worsen NAT filtering: Protocols like Teredo allow inbound connections from the Internet. To support this, the tunnel uses techniques (like STUN) to make the NAT learn of incoming sources by sending "bubbles." This removes the NAT's Address-Dependent or Address-and-Port-Dependent filtering, allowing any attacker to send packets through the tunnel client's port without being a previous destination.

The mitigation is to minimize tunnel use: activate tunnels only when needed, deactivate them promptly, run a host firewall on the tunnel interface, and prefer native connectivity over tunneled when available.
sections.plainLanguage: Open holes in NAT are like doors in a building's perimeter. Tunnels keep these doors open longer than normal, making them easier to find. Internet-facing tunnels like Teredo remove the guard that normally checks who enters, allowing attackers to knock.

sections.title: Information Leakage Through Tunnel Addresses
sections.content:
Guessable addresses: Some tunnel protocols use well-defined address ranges or algorithmic address construction. Teredo and 6to4 use predictable address spaces. Tunnel brokers use well-known server addresses. This reduces the search space for attackers; they can scan predictable ranges more efficiently than random IPv6 addresses.

Platform and software profiling: An attacker seeing a Teredo address knows the host is likely running Windows (Teredo is default on Windows). If the server field in the address resolves to a Microsoft server, the Windows assumption is stronger. This information helps attackers target attacks: rather than blindly scanning, an attacker can focus on known Windows vulnerabilities.

Organizational inference: The external IPv4 address embedded in addresses like Teredo reveals the ISP or organization. This is not new to tunneling but is a minor additional disclosure.

Mitigations include randomizing server configurations during installation, using random values for otherwise unused address fields, and tunnel protocols designed with less guessable address structures. Administrators can also randomize tunnel client ports to reduce profiling based on port patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunnel addresses can reveal what operating system you are running and which company is your Internet provider. Attackers use this to guess which attacks would work before even trying anything.

sections.title: Man-in-the-Middle Risks
sections.content:
The problem: If an attacker can change a tunnel client's server setting (or poison DNS to redirect the client), and the tunnel is not authenticated, the attacker becomes a man-in-the-middle. The attacker's server can monitor the client's communications and potentially impersonate remote peers.

Phishing scenario: A malicious server provides correct service most of the time but intercepts certain connections. A user types their bank's URL, which resolves to an IP address. The client uses the tunnel to reach the bank's IP, but the malicious tunnel server places itself in the data path. The server then presents a fake bank login page, stealing credentials.

Defense: The client should authenticate the tunnel server or the means by which the server's address is determined. SSL VPNs use HTTPS to authenticate the server. Router Advertisements sent over tunnels can use SEND (Secure Neighbor Discovery) to verify the server's identity. On the host, changing tunnel server settings should require privilege, and the current setting should be visible without privilege, making silent changes detectable.

Preferring native IPv4 over tunneled IPv6 (as recommended in RFC 3484) also reduces this risk by reducing tunnel use.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone switches your tunnel server setting, you might unknowingly send all your traffic through their computer. They can read everything you send and show you fake websites. Make sure your computer verifies the tunnel server is trustworthy before using it.
